deck.title: Redox Processes: Electron Transfer & Changes in Oxidation Number (Oxidation State)

front_blocks.md: Define **oxidation number**.

back_blocks.md: An **oxidation number** (or oxidation state) is a number assigned to each atom in a compound to track electron transfer. A positive value indicates loss of electrons and a negative value indicates gain of electrons.

front_blocks.md: What is the oxidation number of sulfur in SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>?

back_blocks.md: Oxygen contributes 4 x (-2) = -8. The overall charge is -2. So S = -2 - (-8) = **+6**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The oxidation number of oxygen is always -2 in all compounds.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Oxygen is usually -2, but it is -1 in peroxides (e.g. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) and +2 in F<sub>2</sub>O, where fluorine is more electronegative.

front_blocks.md: The sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral compound is **..........**  . The sum in an ion equals **..........**  . The oxidation number of any uncombined element is **..........** .

back_blocks.md: The sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral compound is **zero**. The sum in an ion equals **the charge on the ion**. The oxidation number of any uncombined element is **zero**.

front_blocks.md: What is the oxidation number of nitrogen in NH<sub>3</sub>?

back_blocks.md: Hydrogen contributes 3 x (+1) = +3. Overall charge = 0. So N = 0 - 3 = **-3**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Hydrogen always has an oxidation number of +1.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Hydrogen is +1 in most compounds, but -1 in metal hydrides such as NaH, where it is the more electronegative element.

front_blocks.md: Define **fixed oxidation number**.

back_blocks.md: Some elements have **fixed oxidation numbers** in compounds. Group 1 metals are always +1, Group 2 metals are always +2, and fluorine is always -1 because it is the most electronegative element.

front_blocks.md: In ClO<sub>2</sub><sup>-</sup>, oxygen contributes **..........**  and the overall charge is -1. The oxidation number of chlorine is therefore **..........** .

back_blocks.md: In ClO<sub>2</sub><sup>-</sup>, oxygen contributes **-4** and the overall charge is -1. The oxidation number of chlorine is therefore **+3**.

front_blocks.md: What is the oxidation number of phosphorus in P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>?

back_blocks.md: Five O atoms = 5 x (-2) = -10. Overall charge = 0. So 2 P = +10, giving each P atom an oxidation number of **+5**.

cards.front_md: What is the oxidation number of phosphorus in P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>?
cards.back_md: Five O atoms = 5 x (-2) = -10. Overall charge = 0. So 2 P = +10, giving each P atom an oxidation number of **+5**.

front_blocks.md: Define **disproportionation reaction**.

back_blocks.md: A **disproportionation reaction** is one in which the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced. For example, chlorine reacting with hot concentrated NaOH forms Cl<sup>-</sup> (reduced) and ClO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> (oxidised).

cards.front_md: Define **disproportionation reaction**.
cards.back_md: A **disproportionation reaction** is one in which the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced. For example, chlorine reacting with hot concentrated NaOH forms Cl<sup>-</sup> (reduced) and ClO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> (oxidised).

front_blocks.md: In the reaction Cu<sup>2+</sup> + Mg → Mg<sup>2+</sup> + Cu, which species is oxidised and which is reduced? Use oxidation numbers to justify your answer.

back_blocks.md: **Mg** is **oxidised** (oxidation number 0 to +2, loss of electrons). **Cu**<sup>**2+**</sup> is **reduced** (oxidation number +2 to 0, gain of electrons).

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Oxidation involves the gain of electrons.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Oxidation is the loss of electrons (and causes an increase in oxidation number). The acronym OIL RIG (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain) is a useful memory aid.

front_blocks.md: Oxidation causes an **..........**  in oxidation number. Reduction causes a **..........**  in oxidation number. In a redox reaction, **..........**  and **..........**  always occur together.

back_blocks.md: Oxidation causes an **increase** in oxidation number. Reduction causes a **decrease** in oxidation number. In a redox reaction, **oxidation** and **reduction** always occur together.

front_blocks.md: Define **redox reaction**.

back_blocks.md: A **redox reaction** is a reaction in which oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously. One species loses electrons (is oxidised) while another gains electrons (is reduced).

cards.front_md: Define **redox reaction**.

front_blocks.md: List the five steps for balancing a redox equation using oxidation numbers.

back_blocks.md: 1. Write the unbalanced equation and identify atoms that **change in oxidation number**. 2. Deduce the **oxidation number changes**. 3. **Balance the oxidation number changes**. 4. **Balance the charges**. 5. **Balance the atoms**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In the reaction 2Na + Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2NaCl, chlorine is oxidised.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Chlorine is reduced (oxidation number changes from 0 to -1, a gain of electrons). Sodium is oxidised (0 to +1, a loss of electrons).

front_blocks.md: Oxidation can be defined as the gain of **..........**  , the loss of **..........**  , or the loss of **..........** . Reduction is the reverse of each of these.

back_blocks.md: Oxidation can be defined as the gain of **oxygen**, the loss of **hydrogen**, or the loss of **electrons**. Reduction is the reverse of each of these.

front_blocks.md: In the reaction 3Cl<sub>2</sub> + 6OH<sup>-</sup> → 5Cl<sup>-</sup> + ClO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O, why is this classified as a disproportionation reaction?

back_blocks.md: **Chlorine** (oxidation number 0 in Cl<sub>2</sub>) is both **reduced** to Cl<sup>-</sup> (oxidation number -1) and **oxidised** to ClO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> (oxidation number +5). The same element undergoes both oxidation and reduction.

cards.front_md: In the reaction 3Cl<sub>2</sub> + 6OH<sup>-</sup> → 5Cl<sup>-</sup> + ClO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O, why is this classified as a disproportionation reaction?
cards.back_md: **Chlorine** (oxidation number 0 in Cl<sub>2</sub>) is both **reduced** to Cl<sup>-</sup> (oxidation number -1) and **oxidised** to ClO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> (oxidation number +5). The same element undergoes both oxidation and reduction.

front_blocks.md: Define **oxidising agent**.

back_blocks.md: An **oxidising agent** is a substance that oxidises another species by causing it to lose electrons. The oxidising agent itself gains electrons and is reduced, so its oxidation number decreases.

front_blocks.md: In the reaction Mg + Fe<sup>2+</sup> → Mg<sup>2+</sup> + Fe, which species is the oxidising agent and why?

back_blocks.md: **Fe**<sup>**2+**</sup> is the **oxidising agent**. Its oxidation number decreases from +2 to 0 (it gains electrons and is reduced), which means it causes Mg to be oxidised.

cards.front_md: In the reaction Mg + Fe<sup>2+</sup> → Mg<sup>2+</sup> + Fe, which species is the oxidising agent and why?
cards.back_md: **Fe**<sup>**2+**</sup> is the **oxidising agent**. Its oxidation number decreases from +2 to 0 (it gains electrons and is reduced), which means it causes Mg to be oxidised.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A reducing agent loses electrons and its oxidation number increases.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
A reducing agent is itself oxidised in the process of reducing another species. It donates electrons, causing its oxidation number to rise.

front_blocks.md: An oxidising agent is itself **..........**  in a redox reaction. A reducing agent is itself **..........** . Both an oxidising and a **..........**  agent must be present for a redox reaction to occur.

back_blocks.md: An oxidising agent is itself **reduced** in a redox reaction. A reducing agent is itself **oxidised**. Both an oxidising and a **reducing** agent must be present for a redox reaction to occur.

front_blocks.md: Define **reducing agent**.

back_blocks.md: A **reducing agent** is a substance that reduces another species by donating electrons to it. The reducing agent itself is oxidised, losing electrons and increasing in oxidation number.

front_blocks.md: How are Roman numerals used in naming compounds of transition metals? Give two examples.

back_blocks.md: **Roman numerals** indicate the **oxidation state** of the transition metal. For example, FeO is iron(II) oxide (Fe<sup>2+</sup>) and Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is iron(III) oxide (Fe<sup>3+</sup>).

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In the reaction Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2Br<sup>-</sup> → 2Cl<sup>-</sup> + Br<sub>2</sub>, Br<sup>-</sup> acts as an oxidising agent.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Br<sup>-</sup> is the reducing agent. Its oxidation number increases from -1 to 0 (it is oxidised). Cl<sub>2</sub> is the oxidising agent, being reduced from 0 to -1.

Br<sup>-</sup> is the reducing agent. Its oxidation number increases from -1 to 0 (it is oxidised). Cl<sub>2</sub> is the oxidising agent, being reduced from 0 to -1.

front_blocks.md: The systematic name of FeCl<sub>2</sub> is **..........**  because iron has an oxidation number of **..........** . The systematic name of NO<sub>2</sub> is **..........**  oxide.

back_blocks.md: The systematic name of FeCl<sub>2</sub> is **iron(II) chloride** because iron has an oxidation number of **+2**. The systematic name of NO<sub>2</sub> is **nitrogen(IV)** oxide.

front_blocks.md: Can the same substance act as both an oxidising agent and a reducing agent? Give a brief explanation.

back_blocks.md: Yes. Some substances can act as either an **oxidising** or a **reducing agent** depending on the reaction conditions and the species they react with. Their role is determined by the relative oxidising and reducing power of the other reactant.
